title: Inquest offers more proof that RCMP shouldn't investigate itself
article: If the Ian Bush case didn't convince people that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police shouldn't be investigating itself, then the Kevin St. Arnaud case certainly should.

Bush was the 22-year-old British Columbia mill worker who was shot to death under mysterious circumstances by a rookie RCMP officer in a Houston police station. The case raised many concerns, since a number of RCMP policies were violated, and since the investigation by the Prince George Mounties took 10 months to complete despite it concerning a relatively simple shooting involving two people. Ultimately, though, the Crown decided not to lay any charges against the officer.

Fortunately, a coroner's inquest into Bush's death -- which has yet to be scheduled -- might resolve some of the mystery surrounding the death, and might reveal the problems associated with the RCMP investigating itself. That is precisely what happened during the inquest into the death of Kevin St. Arnaud, which wrapped up last week.

In the early morning of Dec. 19, 2004, St. Arnaud, a 29-year-old drugstore robbery suspect, was shot three times by 22-year-old RCMP Const. Ryan Sheremetta. Sheremetta had been chasing St. Arnaud through an icy soccer field in Vanderhoof, and said that he slipped and fell on his back, that St. Arnaud advanced toward him and that Sheremetta fired the fatal shots when St. Arnaud was "basically . . . over top of me."

Although the RCMP officers investigating the incident admitted there were inaccuracies in Sheremetta's account of the events, they nevertheless concluded that he acted in self-defence, and the Crown decided against laying charges.

The inquest heard a very different story. Sheremetta's partner, Const. Colleen Erickson, who is a 24-year police veteran, testified that Sheremetta was standing up, in a "police shooting stance," when the shots were fired. A civilian eyewitness had similar testimony.

Further, a blood specialties expert testified that, based on the blood patterns found on the snow, St. Arnaud couldn't have been moving toward Sheremetta, but must have been standing still when he was shot. Plus, a forensic expert testified that St. Arnaud couldn't have been over top of Sheremetta, but had to be at least two feet away at the time of the shooting.

The evidence from a forensic pathologist corroborated this testimony. The pathologist testified that the bullets entered St. Arnaud's body in a downward trajectory of 30 to 45 degrees, which means Sheremetta was likely standing up when the shots were fired.

None of this means that Sheremetta is guilty of anything, of course, since it's not the role of a coroner's inquest to lay blame. (Shortly before the conclusion of the inquest, the Crown did, however, say that it was willing to review the file if new information was produced by the inquest.)

But the inquest testimony does confirm that there appear to be serious inaccuracies in Sheremetta's recollection of events. On a broader level, the inquest testimony adds to the mounting evidence that the RCMP shouldn't be investigating itself, at least in cases where an officer causes the death of another person.

After all, the RCMP's reputation has been seriously battered by the Bush and St. Arnaud cases, and if people lose respect for our national police force, then it will be much more difficult for officers to do what is already a difficult job. For the good of both the public and the RCMP, it's time to consider allowing an independent body to investigate cases like these.
